# frost — SPEC

## Maturity

**Grade:** 4 · S4 E2 A1 H3 P3 · limited by scope (mvp) *(generated by `zig build gen-catalog`)*

**Scope:** mvp — ZcashFoundation/frost frost-core 3.0.0, secp256k1 suite only (surveyed 2026-09-30)

**Audit:** review 2026-10-08 · mutation 2026-11-25 (150/157, 7 eq) · src 7cf6e292dcd5bc50

**Hardening:** fuzz 2026-10-10 (200,000-run budget per harness clean (`frost-protocol` at its scale, 1,000), FROST_FUZZ) · ct 2026-09-09 (ctgrind)

**Performance:** not measured

**Known defects:** none recorded

**Downstream consumer:** no

FROST (Flexible Round-Optimized Schnorr Threshold signatures), RFC 9591,
**secp256k1/SHA-256 ciphersuite (§6.5) only**; see [README.md](README.md)
for purpose and API. Provenance: see [NOTICE](NOTICE).

**Where we are ahead:** the only RFC-vector-anchored FROST in Zig that we found (the one other Zig FROST, `bsvz-frost`, was not examined beyond its description): every intermediate value of RFC 9591 Appendix E.5 is pinned byte-exact (binding factors, nonces, shares, final signature); nominally distinct wire types (`SigningShare` vs `SignatureShare`) so a share cannot be passed where a signature share belongs; explicit-randomness inputs so signing is replayable; mutation-audited; ctgrind harness; dead-stack probe; frost-core's distributed key generation (`frost.dkg`), checked against frost-core's published DKG vector. **Where we are behind:** one ciphersuite of the RFC's five (secp256k1 only — the RFC's recommended ristretto255 and the widely deployed Ed25519 are absent) (→ Roadmap); no BIP-340 / Taproot-compatible variant (`frost-secp256k1-tr`, multi-party-sig); no share refresh, repair or re-randomized signatures.

## Design

- **Source of truth**: RFC 9591 (IRTF CFRG, June 2024), consumed directly
  from `https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9591.txt`. Only the
  secp256k1/SHA-256 ciphersuite (§6.5) is in scope — RFC 9591 also
  defines Ed25519 (§6.1), Ed448 (§6.3), ristretto255 (§6.2, the RFC's
  RECOMMENDED ciphersuite), and P-256 (§6.4); none of those are
  scaffolded here. A ristretto255 pass is a reasonable follow-up module
  but a SEPARATE one — different group, different `H1`..`H5`, different
  `Ne`/`Ns` — not an extension of this file.
- **`H1`/`H2`/`H3` are `hash_to_field`, NOT a BIP340-style tagged hash.**
  This is the single most-likely-to-be-gotten-wrong detail in this
  ciphersuite, worth restating outside `root.zig`'s doc comments too: RFC
  9591 §6.5 defines `H1(m) = hash_to_field(m, 1)` per RFC 9380 §5.2, with
  `expand_message_xmd`, SHA-256, `L = 48`, `DST = contextString ||
  "rho"` (similarly `"chal"` for `H2`, `"nonce"` for `H3`). This is a
  DIFFERENT hash construction from `bip340.taggedHash`'s `SHA256(SHA256
  (tag) || SHA256(tag) || msg)` — different preimage shape, different
  domain-separation mechanism (a length-prefixed DST folded into TWO
  compression-function calls via `expand_message_xmd`'s `b_0`/`b_1`/`b_2`
  chaining, not a simple midstate reuse), and a WIDE reduction
  (48 bytes → mod `p`, not a direct 32-byte parse). `H4`/`H5` ARE simple
  tagged SHA-256 (`SHA256(contextString || label || m)`, no
  `expand_message_xmd`) — do not confuse the two hash SHAPES within the
  same ciphersuite. `expand_message_xmd` itself is `sha2.expandMessageXmd`
  (the collection's one RFC 9380 §5.3.1 copy, its K.1–K.3 vectors in `sha2`).
- **Validation of the hash layer**: RFC 9591's own Appendix E.5 vector
  does not publish an `expand_message_xmd`/`hash_to_field` KAT in
  isolation (RFC 9380 has its own separate vector suite for that, not
  embedded here), but it DOES publish `binding_factor_input` →
  `binding_factor` pairs (`H1` applied to a known 129-byte preimage) and
  `hiding_nonce_randomness`/`participant_share` → `hiding_nonce` triples
  (`H3` applied to a known 64-byte preimage) — both exercised byte-exact
  in `kat_test.zig`, which is a real, if indirect, `expand_message_xmd`
  KAT. `H2` shares the identical construction (only the DST label
  differs) and is validated only indirectly, through `round2Sign`'s
  signature-share equation matching the vector's `sig_share` — see "what the vectors do NOT cover" below.
- **BIP340 compatibility — explicit finding: NO.** Restated from
  `root.zig`'s module doc comment (the single most important correctness
  fact for a reader of this module to internalize): this ciphersuite's
  elements are 33-byte SEC1-COMPRESSED points (not BIP340's 32-byte
  x-only/even-y), its signature is 65 bytes `(R, z)` (not BIP340's 64
  bytes `(r, s)`), and its challenge hash `H2` — both preimage shape
  (`33 + 33 + msg`, not `32 + 32 + msg`) AND construction
  (`expand_message_xmd`, not a BIP340 tagged hash) — differs from
  BIP340's. `verify` in this module implements RFC 9591 Appendix B's
  `prime_order_verify` directly; it does not call `bip340.verify`, and no
  amount of encode/decode glue bridges the two (the challenge hash
  itself is different, not just the wire format). The module does not
  depend on `bip340`.
- **Type design — wire types vs. raw `Scalar`**: values that flow "over
  the wire" between participants/the Coordinator (`Identifier`,
  `SigningShare`, `VerifyingShare`/`GroupPublicKey`/`NonceCommitment`
  (all `Element`), `SignatureShare`, `SigningCommitments`, `Signature`)
  are bespoke byte-array-backed structs with `fromBytes`/`toBytes`
  performing RFC 9591's own `DeserializeScalar`/`DeserializeElement`
  validation. Values that are NEVER serialized (`SigningNonces` — RFC
  9591 §5.1: "The nonce value is secret and MUST NOT be shared"; the
  trusted dealer's `secret_key`/`coefficients` in `trustedDealerKeygen`)
  use the raw `Secp256k1.scalar.Scalar` type directly (re-exported as
  `frost.Scalar`), since there is no wire encoding to validate against.
- **`SigningShare`/`SignatureShare` share an identical wire shape** (both
  32-byte big-endian `Scalar`s) but are kept as NOMINALLY DISTINCT Zig
  types via the `ScalarWire(comptime tag: []const u8)` factory, so a call
  site cannot accidentally pass one where the other belongs despite the
  compiler seeing "just 32 bytes" in both cases.
- **Deterministic entry points, no internal RNG** (the task's own
  "critical correctness note", worth preserving here): `round1Commit`
  takes `SigningNonces` directly rather than generating them itself;
  `trustedDealerKeygen` takes `coefficients` directly rather than
  sampling them itself; `nonceGenerate`/`generateNonces` take
  `random_bytes` as an explicit parameter rather than reading a global
  RNG. This is what makes every one of these replayable against RFC 9591
  Appendix E.5's fixed vector — a real deployment's caller is
  responsible for sourcing fresh secure randomness for the `..._random`/
  `coefficients` inputs (see `Secp256k1.scalar.random`/`std.Io`).
- **`Ne = 33`, `Ns = 32`** (RFC 9591 §6.5) are exported as named
  constants (`frost.Ne`, `frost.Ns`) rather than inlined as magic numbers
  throughout — every wire type's `encoded_length` derives from them.
- **Allocator usage**: functions whose output/scratch space scales with
  the number of participants (`computeBindingFactors`,
  `participantsFromCommitmentList`, `encodeGroupCommitmentList`,
  `round2Sign`, `aggregate`, `verifySignatureShare`,
  `trustedDealerKeygen`) take an explicit `allocator: std.mem.Allocator`
  parameter (CONVENTIONS.md §1 item 2: "caller-supplied allocators, no
  hidden globals") — NONE of them reach for a global/page allocator.
  Functions whose output is O(1) regardless of participant count
  (`computeGroupCommitment`, `deriveInterpolatingValue`, `round1Commit`,
  `verify`, `computeChallenge`, `h1`..`h5`, `nonceGenerate`,
  `generateNonces`, `bindingFactorForParticipant`) take no allocator.
- **What the vectors do NOT cover**: RFC 9591 Appendix E.5's secp256k1
  vector does not publish a standalone `group_commitment` or `challenge`
  scalar (unlike `binding_factor_input`/`binding_factor`, which ARE
  published per-signer). This is confirmed by direct reading of the RFC
  text, not an oversight in transcription. Consequently
  `computeGroupCommitment` is checked only via `aggregate`'s `R` output
  matching the vector's published `sig`'s first 33 bytes, and
  `computeChallenge`/`h2` is checked only via `round2Sign`'s
  signature-share equation reproducing the vector's published
  `sig_share` byte-exact (both are complete, correct checks — just
  indirect ones, composed rather than isolated).

## Threat model

- **Signing-share secrecy** (`SigningShare`, `SigningNonces`): the
  central secret this scheme protects is the group secret `s` — no
  single participant's `sk_i` (nor, before combination, any
  `MIN_PARTICIPANTS - 1`-sized subset of them) should leak `s` or enable
  forging a signature. This is Shamir's information-theoretic guarantee,
  not something the Zig implementation can strengthen or weaken by
  itself — but the implementation MUST NOT introduce a side channel that
  leaks `sk_i`/nonce values through timing (RFC 9591 §7.1 "Side-Channel
  Mitigations" — the same category of concern `bip340`'s doc comments
  flag for `d`/`k`). `Secp256k1.scalar`'s field ops are std's own
  constant-time implementation; this module introduces no additional
  branches on secret scalars (each core's doc comment flags which
  operands are secret; ctgrind measures `round1Commit` and `round2Sign`, see *Verification*).
- **Nonce reuse** (RFC 9591 §7.3 "Nonce Reuse Attacks"): reusing a
  `(hiding_nonce, binding_nonce)` pair across two `round2Sign` calls for
  the same participant is a KEY-RECOVERY vulnerability (classic
  Schnorr/ECDSA nonce-reuse linear-algebra attack, generalized to the
  threshold setting) — RFC 9591 §5.2 states this as a MUST NOT. This
  module cannot enforce "used exactly once" at the type level (a
  `SigningNonces` value has no built-in single-use marker); a caller
  integrating this module is responsible for deleting/never reusing a
  nonce pair after one `round2Sign` call, exactly as the RFC's own prose
  requires of the CALLER, not the primitive.
- **Identifiable abort / misbehaving participants** (RFC 9591 §5.4):
  FROST provides no robustness — one dishonest signer contributing a bad
  share can only be detected (via `verifySignatureShare`), not tolerated.
  This module exposes `verifySignatureShare` precisely so a Coordinator
  CAN implement this detection, and `aggregateVerified` does it the way
  frost-core's `aggregate` does: verify the aggregate, and only when it
  fails, check every share and name the first bad signer (`culprit`). It
  does not itself decide what to do about a misbehaving participant (out
  of scope, same as the RFC's own stance). `verifySignatureShare` keeps
  the RFC's separate `comm_i` parameter but checks it is `identifier`'s
  entry in `commitment_list` (frost-core reads it from the signing
  package): a different pair is `error.InvalidCommitmentList`, so a share
  is never verified against commitments the binding factors were not
  computed over.
- **Trusted dealer** (RFC 9591 Appendix C, `trustedDealerKeygen`): the
  dealer must generate good randomness, delete `secret_key`/
  `secret_key_shares` after distribution, and keep them confidential
  until distributed — this module's `trustedDealerKeygen` does not (and
  cannot) enforce any of that; it is a pure computation. A deployment
  that must not have a single trusted dealer uses the distributed key
  generation (`frost.dkg`, below), which RFC 9591 itself leaves out.
- **`verify`/`verifySignatureShare` never panic on adversarial input** —
  `verify` returns `bool` (every malformed input is `false`); `verifySignatureShare`
  returns an error union for malformed input and `false` for a well-formed share that does not
  verify; NEITHER treats "doesn't verify"
  as an error condition (mirrors `bip340.verify`'s own convention) —
  important for a Coordinator that must keep running after rejecting one
  bad share, not abort the whole process.

- **`round2Sign` checks its own commitments.** RFC 9591 §5.2: each participant MUST ensure that its
  identifier AND commitments from the first round appear in `commitment_list` (frost-core's `sign`
  returns `IncorrectCommitment`). `round2Sign` recomputes the commitments from `nonces` and compares
  them with the listed pair: `Round2SignError.IncorrectCommitment` when the listed hiding or binding
  commitment differs, `InvalidCommitmentList` when the identifier is absent. A Coordinator could
  otherwise choose this signer's part of `R`.
- **`trustedDealerKeygen` refuses `min_participants < 2`** (RFC 9591 Appendix C.1: a threshold of 1 is
  a constant polynomial, every share equal to the group secret) and zeroes the shares before freeing
  them on an error path.
- **Dead-stack burns.** `generateNonces`, `round1Commit` and `round2Sign` run their work in a
  `noinline` inner function and burn 32 KiB of the stack after it (the share and both nonces would
  otherwise stay readable there; a nonce next to the published signature share is `lambda_i·sk_i`, the
  share). For the same reason `round1Commit`/`round2Sign` take `nonces: *const SigningNonces` (as
  frost-core's `&SigningNonces`) and `signing_share: *const SigningShare`, so no by-value copy of a
  secret is made at the call boundary outside any burn. The burn zeroes with volatile vector stores;
  its buffer is 16-aligned so the frame is not realigned.
- **`verify` guards a canonical `z`.** A hand-built `Signature` (not via `fromBytes`) with `z >= n` would
  verify its reduced twin (std's point multiplication takes the raw 256-bit integer), so `verify` first
  rejects a non-canonical `z`; the check is unobservable through the equation alone, since a `z`
  that passes it needs `z < 2^256 − n`, about 2^-128.
- **`vssVerify` (RFC 9591 Appendix C.2).** `vssVerify(share: *const ParticipantShare, vss_commitment:
  []const Element) !bool` checks a dealer share against the Feldman commitment by Horner's rule over the
  commitment points (equal to the RFC's sum of `C_j * i^j`). `false` on any mismatch, a malformed
  commitment element, a zero share or a sum that is the identity; only an empty `vss_commitment` is an
  error (`VssVerifyError.InvalidParameters`). The share enters only the constant-time base-point
  multiplication; the commitments and identifier powers are public and use the variable-time public one.

## Out of scope

- Ristretto255/Ed25519/Ed448/P-256 ciphersuites (RFC 9591 §6.1-§6.4) —
  not yet, see Roadmap; each needs its own module (different
  group/hash/`Ne`/`Ns`).
- Distributed/removed-Coordinator deployment shapes (RFC 9591 §7.5) — the
  Coordinator role here is left to the caller/consumer, same as the RFC's
  own framing (this module supplies the per-role FUNCTIONS, not a
  network protocol or role-assignment policy).

## Distributed key generation (`dkg.zig`)

`frost.dkg` is frost-core's `dkg` module (the reference: ZcashFoundation/frost, frost-core v3.0.0,
`frost-core/src/keys/dkg.rs`, read; MIT OR Apache-2.0): the FROST paper's two-round Pedersen DKG with a
Schnorr proof of knowledge of each participant's constant term (Komlo–Goldberg 2020, Figure 1). RFC 9591
specifies none (its Appendix C is the trusted dealer); the construction, the challenge hash and the checks
are frost-core's.

- `part1(allocator, out: *Round1SecretPackage, identifier, max_signers, min_signers, coefficients: []const
  Scalar, nonce: *const Scalar) !Round1Package`: Feldman commitment `φ_j = a_j·G` to the `min_signers`
  coefficients (`a_0` first) and the proof `(R, μ)`, `R = k·G`, `μ = k + a_0·c`,
  `c = HDKG(SerializeScalar(i) || SerializeElement(φ_0) || SerializeElement(R))`; `frost.hdkg` is
  `hash_to_field` with DST `contextString || "dkg"` (frost-core's `HDKG` for this ciphersuite). The
  randomness is the caller's, as in the rest of the module.
- `part2(allocator, out: *Round2SecretPackage, secret: *const Round1SecretPackage, round1_packages: []const
  Round1Received, culprit: ?*Identifier) ![]Round2Package`: frost-core's checks in its order — exactly
  `max_signers - 1` packages (`IncorrectNumberOfPackages`), the own identifier absent
  (`UnknownIdentifier`), every commitment of length `min_signers` (`IncorrectNumberOfCommitments`), then
  each proof (`InvalidProofOfKnowledge`, sender in `culprit`) — and the shares `f_i(ℓ)` to send privately.
  frost-core's packages are a map keyed by sender, so a repeated sender cannot occur there; here it is
  `DuplicatedIdentifier` (frost-core's name for a repeated identifier elsewhere).
- `part3(allocator, out: *KeyPackage, secret: *const Round2SecretPackage, round1_packages, round2_packages:
  []const Round2Received, culprit) !PublicKeyPackage`: counts and sender sets (`IncorrectPackage` for a
  round-1 sender with no share), each share checked with `vssVerify` against its sender's commitment
  (`InvalidSecretShare`, sender in `culprit`), `s_i = Σ f_ℓ(i)`, the group key `Σ φ_ℓ0` and every
  participant's verifying share from the summed commitments (ascending by identifier, as frost-core's
  `BTreeMap`). `InvalidCommitment` covers an identity in the summed commitment (cancelling polynomials;
  frost-core fails there on serialization).
- `verifyProofOfKnowledge(sender, package) bool` is public (frost-core's is `internals`-only) for a
  coordinator that relays round-1 packages.
- Secrets: `coefficients`, `nonce`, the received shares; every part runs one `noinline` frame down and
  burns the stack after it (`burn.zig`, shared with signing); the secret packages and `Round2Package`
  lists have wiping `deinit`/`freeRound2Packages`. The `KeyPackage` feeds `generateNonces`/`round2Sign`
  directly.
- Channels are the caller's (DKG requirement): round-1 packages over an authenticated broadcast, round-2
  shares over confidential authenticated point-to-point channels; `sender` is what the channel vouches for.
- Not offered: frost-core's serde/postcard package encoding (a versioned header around the same
  elements and scalars) — the packages here are plain values whose parts have this module's codecs.

Tests (`dkg_test.zig`): frost-core v3.0.0's published DKG vector for this ciphersuite
(`frost-secp256k1/tests/helpers/vectors_dkg.json`, 2-of-3), run as frost-core's own `check_dkg_keygen`
does — each participant's polynomial reproduces its published commitment, `part2` accepts the two
published proofs made by frost-core (pinning `HDKG`'s DST and preimage) and sends the published shares,
`part3` on the published received shares gives the published signing share, verifying share, group key
and all three verifying shares (an RFC model in Python checked the vector first); the published proofs
refused under another sender, another commitment or a bent `μ`; a 3-of-5 run whose output every
participant agrees on, reconstructs `Σ a_i0` from any 3 shares (and all 5), and signs and verifies with
3 signers; a bent proof and a bent share refused with the sender named; every count and identifier check;
no leak under an allocation failure in any part.

## The ten threshold-specific cryptographic cores

All ten are implemented in `root.zig`; each function's doc comment spells out the exact RFC 9591
construction (`vssVerify`, Appendix C.2, is documented under *Design*):

- `deriveInterpolatingValue` (§4.2) — the Lagrange coefficient at `x=0`.
  THE threshold-specific primitive; everything else built on top of it
  is "ordinary" (n-of-n) Schnorr math.
- `computeBindingFactors` (§4.4) — the anti-forgery construction tying
  each signer's binding nonce to the whole commitment set.
- `computeGroupCommitment` (§4.5) — sums each signer's
  `hiding_nonce_commitment + binding_factor * binding_nonce_commitment`.
- `round1Commit` (§5.1's public-commitment half) — `ScalarBaseMult` of
  each supplied nonce.
- `round2Sign` (§5.2) — the signature-share equation:
  `hiding_nonce + binding_nonce*binding_factor + lambda_i*sk_i*challenge`.
- `aggregate` (§5.3) — `R = computeGroupCommitment(...)`,
  `z = sum(sig_shares)`.
- `verifySignatureShare` (§5.3) — the per-share verification equation;
  `aggregateVerified` (§5.3/§5.4) — `aggregate`, `verify`, and on failure
  the share that does not verify.
- `verify` (Appendix B `prime_order_verify`) — the aggregate-signature
  verification equation (NOT `bip340.verify` — see "BIP340 compatibility"
  above).
- `trustedDealerKeygen` / `secretShareCombine` (Appendix C) — Shamir
  split (`secret_share_shard` + `vss_commit`) and combine
  (`secret_share_combine` via `polynomial_interpolate_constant`).

`kat_test.zig`'s assertions (one per core, against RFC 9591 Appendix E.5's
published intermediate/final values) are the acceptance check.

## Verification

Run `scripts/modtest frost` (the dead-stack probe runs in ReleaseFast only; Debug and ReleaseSafe fill
`undefined`, so it is skipped there). Test classes:

- **RFC 9591 Appendix E.5 KAT** (`kat_vectors.zig`, `kat_test.zig`), byte-exact: `H1` and `H3` on the
  published preimages (an indirect `expand_message_xmd` KAT), `H4`/`H5` inside the binding-factor input,
  `round1Commit`, `computeBindingFactors`, `trustedDealerKeygen`, `secretShareCombine` over every 2-subset,
  `round2Sign` for both signers, `aggregate` to the published signature, `verify` and
  `verifySignatureShare` accepting the published values and rejecting a tampered `z`, `R` or share; an end-to-end
  (2,3) round trip.
- **What the vectors cannot see:** a t = 3 sharing checked share by share against `vss_commitment`
  (Feldman; the published t = 2 vector cannot see the Horner coefficient order or which coefficient a
  commitment is taken from), `vssVerify` on dealt shares and on a tampered share, commitment and
  identifier, `secretShareCombine` refusing one share and a repeated identifier, `Identifier.fromBytes(0)`
  and `Element.fromPoint(identity)`, `trustedDealerKeygen` below threshold 2, `round2Sign` refusing a
  commitment list that does not carry its own commitments (and a zero nonce reporting
  `IncorrectCommitment`), the `deinit` wipes.
- **Fuzz:** three harnesses run by testkit's deterministic driver as `FROST_FUZZ` (`src/fuzz_test.zig`,
  `_ONLY` selects by name): `frost-verify` (the published signature with a few octets replaced; `verify`
  never panics), `frost-wire` (decoders reject what is not canonical and re-encode what they accept),
  `frost-protocol` (a (t,n) signing round trip is accepted, damaged signatures and shares are not), each
  with a fixed seed loop and reach checks in every test run.
- **Dead stack:** `src/stackprobe_test.zig` paints the region below the call and scans it for the signing
  share, both nonces and their negations in big-endian, little-endian and in-memory images after
  `generateNonces`, `round1Commit` and `round2Sign`, with a negative control (public data only) and a
  positive control (parks the share in a local).
- **Constant time:** ctgrind harness `src/ctgrind_harness.zig`, targets `commit` (`round1Commit`) and `sign`
  (`round2Sign`), rows in `scripts/checks/ctgrind-expected.tsv`.
- **Audit:** the card's `**Audit:**` line is the current score, cumulative over the last whole-module
  mutation run and the delta runs after it.
- **Example:** `example/main.zig` drives dealer, two participants and the Coordinator through the published
  module only.
- **Delta mutation 2026-11-25:** 81 mutants over the new `dkg.zig` (all of it) and the `root.zig` functions it touched; 77 killed, 4 equivalent. The first stack probes of the DKG parts found their frames 33-36 KB deep against the 32 KiB burn (residue below the burn after `part3`); fixed 2026-11-26 with a 64 KiB DKG burn, and the three skip-the-burn mutants plus four heap-wipe mutants are killed by the ReleaseFast probes.

## Anchoring

**Anchor grade:** class B · oracle EXTERNAL

- **Class B** — published cryptographic or algorithmic construction with published vectors.
- **Oracle EXTERNAL** — published vectors, goldens captured from a foreign implementation, or a test run against a live foreign peer.

**What the tests actually contain.** RFC 9591 Appendix E.5 official KAT, byte-exact (README/SPEC)

## Backlog / deferred

None open.

## Roadmap

- **ristretto255 and Ed25519 ciphersuites (RFC 9591 §6.2 / §6.1)** — ristretto255 is the RFC's recommended suite and Ed25519 is what most FROST deployments (and `frost-ed25519` users) run; today a non-secp256k1 user has nothing. SPEC "Out of scope" says a separate module per suite; effort: medium each (different `H1`..`H5`, `Ne`/`Ns`), `ct25519` supplies the group. Fits CONVENTIONS §2.
  Size: a new module per suite (one week each with RFC 9591 Appendix E.1/E.2 KATs); needs a group abstraction over `ct25519`.
- **BIP-340-compatible (Taproot) secp256k1 variant** — `frost-secp256k1-tr` and multi-party-sig produce signatures a Bitcoin node accepts; ours are explicitly not BIP-340 (65-byte, 33-byte points). Effort: medium (x-only key/nonce parity handling and BIP-340 challenge). Fits §2.
  Size: one to two weeks (x-only keys, even-y nonce/key negation through both rounds, BIP-340 challenge, frost-secp256k1-tr vectors).
- **Share refresh / repair / re-randomized FROST** — available in frost-core; needed for long-lived custody keys. Effort: medium each. Fits §2. Lower priority than the four items above.
  Size: weeks (three sub-protocols, each with frost-core vectors).
